title: Women’s productive and social roles

blocks.heading: Women’s productive and social roles
blocks.text: Women’s labour in rural societies has included food production, farming, processing, household provision and community activity. Roles vary across time, place and households. Unpaid work contributes to well-being even when it is absent from wage records; a role description is not a justification for unequal opportunity.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Labour
blocks.text: Women contribute physical and mental labour in paid and unpaid activities. Counting wages alone can conceal food preparation, care or productive household work, so assess tasks and time rather than assuming no earnings means no contribution.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Food production
blocks.text: Women can contribute through planting, tending, harvesting, processing and distributing food. Access to land, tools, time and decision-making affects this contribution. Work performed does not establish control over its product or income.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Family welfare
blocks.text: Care, food preparation, water collection and household organisation support family welfare. Unequal caring burdens can restrict time for learning or paid work. Sharing responsibilities or improving services can expand choices without devaluing care.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Read the practical connection
blocks.text: Explain why wage records can understate women’s contribution to family welfare. They can omit unpaid care, food and household production that support well-being. No recorded wage therefore does not establish no work or contribution.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect to Rural Development (5.1) and modern roles (6.2). Separate actual work, access to resources and decision-making influence. Historical mechanisms here are illustrative; no uniform experience or current legal rule is assumed.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
